npx create-react-app FirstMobileApp --mobile
flutter create FirstMobileApp
npm init expo-cli FirstMobileApp

prompt: After running `npx expo start`, what does pressing the `i` key in the terminal do?
choices: Installs the app's native dependencies
Opens the app in the iOS Simulator

prompt: Why does an Image component in React Native usually need explicit width and height set in its style, unlike a plain web tag?
choices: React Native images are always square, so dimensions must be forced manually
The layout engine (Yoga) needs to know a box's size upfront and doesn't read the image file's intrinsic dimensions the way a browser does by default
Images are not supported natively and are rendered as text placeholders without explicit sizing
Expo requires all images to be pre-compiled into the app binary at a fixed pixel size

prompt: In the React Navigation example, how does the DetailsScreen receive the userId value passed from ProfileScreen?
choices: Through a global variable shared between screens
Via route.params.userId, after ProfileScreen calls navigation.navigate('Details', { userId: 42 })
By importing ProfileScreen's state directly into DetailsScreen
Through a URL query string parsed by the browser

prompt: What is the real, non-superficial similarity between useState in a web React component and useState in a React Native component?
choices: Both compile down to the same native machine code
Both are the exact same hook from the same 'react' package, following the same 'UI is a function of state, re-rendered when state changes' model and the same rules about call order
They share a name but behave completely differently under the hood with no real overlap
React Native's useState only works inside class components, unlike the web version

prompt: Why does a React Native component use onPress on a Pressable instead of onClick on a DOM element?
choices: onClick is deprecated in all modern JavaScript and was replaced everywhere by onPress
There is no DOM in React Native; a tap is a touch gesture interpreted by the native gesture responder system and reported as a synthetic event, not a browser MouseEvent
onPress only works with Flutter widgets, not React Native ones
Pressable cannot detect touches, so onPress is purely decorative

prompt: Which statement about testing an app in the iOS Simulator is FALSE?

The simulator runs on your development machine's CPU, not real phone hardware, so performance is not representative
The simulator can fully and accurately test real push notifications exactly as a physical device would
The simulator fakes the camera feed rather than using a real camera

Email the App.js file to the phone and open it in a text editor

Push the project to GitHub and have the phone browser load the raw source files directly
